question: American Thanksgiving has a roughly fixed menu (turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, mashed potato, pumpkin pie) that feels timelessly traditional. Most was assembled in the 1800s. The 1621 Plymouth feast (the supposed model) had wildfowl and venison, little of the modern menu. What does this reveal?
answer: Culinary tradition is often a recent construction projected backward - holiday menus codified in particular moments then narrated as ancient
choices: Culinary tradition is often a recent construction projected backward - holiday menus codified in particular moments then narrated as ancient
Culinary tradition is reliably ancient - holiday menus and regional cuisines preserved from earliest origins by careful oral tradition
Culinary tradition reflects only nutrition science - holiday menus determined by what crops were nutritionally needed at the time
Culinary tradition is geographically determined - holiday menus fixed by what grew locally and never changed across centuries
context: The Thanksgiving menu was assembled in the Lincoln era and Victorian magazines (Sarah Josepha Hale, Godey's Lady's Book). The 1621 Plymouth feast had wildfowl, venison, corn porridge. The 'timeless' menu is a 19th-century construction. The broader lesson: culinary tradition is often a recent construction projected backward - true of Italian tomato cuisine, French haute cuisine, American regional dishes.

question: In the marble-quarry village of Colonnata in Tuscany, an ancient tradition packs slabs of pure pork back-fat in marble basins with sea salt, garlic, rosemary, and herbs. What does this show?
answer: Whole-animal-use ethic since even pure fat is honored as a delicacy
choices: Whole-animal-use ethic since even pure fat is honored as a delicacy
Roman cooking valued only luxury cuts so fat was for slaves not aged
Marble was the only material that resisted fat-staining for long aging
Catholic fasting permitted lard but not muscle, driving the lardo path
context: Lardo di Colonnata IGP: pure pork back-fat cured in marble basins with sea salt, garlic, rosemary, pepper, herbs. Tradition dates to medieval marble quarries. Fat as finished delicacy.

question: Excavations at Pompeii, Cadiz (ancient Gades), Lixus in Morocco, and other Roman ports uncovered garum factories — stone vats where small fish lacto-fermented in salt for months. The factories shipped amphorae of the salty sauce empire-wide. Apicius's 1st-century cookbook calls for garum constantly. What does this reveal?
answer: The Roman Mediterranean economy ran on industrial fermentation infrastructure for everyday seasoning as central as roads and aqueducts were
choices: The Roman Mediterranean economy ran on industrial fermentation infrastructure for everyday seasoning as central as roads and aqueducts were
The Roman Empire substituted garum for salt across its territories; the trade was a workaround for salt shortages not a culinary preference
Garum was a religious offering used only at temples; the wide distribution reflects imperial cult observance not actual culinary use at home
Garum was a luxury good for wealthy Roman elites only; the factories were small-scale boutique production not industrial in real sense
context: Roman garum was industrial-scale fermented fish sauce. Factories at Pompeii, Cadiz (Garum Sociorum, the brand), Lixus, Tingis, Baelo Claudia — large stone vats, amphorae shipping across the empire. Apicius's De Re Coquinaria cites it constantly. Modern relatives: Southeast Asian fish sauce, colatura.

question: Pacific Northwest Native peoples — Chinook, Coast Salish, Tlingit, Haida — built civilizations partly on salmon preservation. Salmon was caught in fish weirs in summer, smoked on cedar racks over slow alder fires for days, stored for winter. Some estimates put pre-contact salmon consumption at hundreds of pounds per person yearly. What does this reveal?
answer: Pre-contact Pacific Northwest civilizations were dense settled and technologically sophisticated; hierarchical societies depended on salmon
choices: Pre-contact Pacific Northwest civilizations were dense settled and technologically sophisticated; hierarchical societies depended on salmon
Pre-contact Pacific Northwest civilizations were nomadic and small-scale; salmon was opportunistic catch not a foundation of any society
Pre-contact Pacific Northwest civilizations had no preservation technology; consumed salmon fresh only with racks post-contact arrival
Pre-contact Pacific Northwest civilizations relied on agricultural staples; salmon preservation was a minor supplement to garden plots
context: Pacific Northwest Native peoples (Chinook, Coast Salish, Tlingit, Haida, Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth) built dense, settled, hierarchical civilizations on salmon-preservation backbone. Cedar smoking racks, fish weirs, smokehouses, dugout canoes. Pre-contact caloric load: ~300-500 lb salmon/person/year. Potlatch economies, cedar architecture.
